title: Nitzavim: all of you (Deuteronomy 29:9–10)
hookLine: everyone stands in the covenant, leaders and woodcutters and water-drawers alike

cards: At any big gathering, a wedding, a graduation, a funeral, someone is at the front. Someone has the good seats. And someone is out back, in the kitchen, clearing plates, parking cars, carrying folding chairs.
Nobody photographs them. Without them the day doesn't happen. The portion called Nitzavim opens with a crowd like that, and it does something unusual.
It names the people in the kitchen. Not as an afterthought, and not at the edge. In the same sentence as the leaders.

teach.b: The portion opens: "Ye are standing this day all of you before the LORD your God: your heads, your tribes, your elders, and your officers, even all the men of Israel."

teach.h: THE HEWER OF WOOD, THE DRAWER OF WATER.
teach.b: Then the list keeps going: the little ones, the wives, the stranger in the camp, "from the hewer of thy wood unto the drawer of thy water." The whole society, top to bottom. All of you.
In the book of Joshua, cutting wood and drawing water is the work given to outsiders with little standing. The people who did it didn't make decisions. They made the fire and the water possible.

And here they stand in the covenant, named, no lower in the sentence's dignity than anyone else. Rashi, following a midrash, says these woodcutters and water-drawers were people from outside who had come to join Israel.
If so, the circle is wider still: newcomers stand in the covenant too.
It matters when this portion is read: on the Shabbat just before Rosh Hashanah, sometimes paired with the next portion, as the season of standing in judgment arrives.
That week, the text puts everyone in the same line.
No one stands alone, and no one is ranked. In a synagogue, the people who set out chairs, cook for the meal afterward, and lock up at night are the reason anyone else can be there at all.
Nitzavim gives them their own line.

how: Nitzavim is read on the Shabbat before Rosh Hashanah, sometimes together with Vayelech, and its opening words, 'you are standing this day, all of you', are often taken up in sermons for the High Holy Days.

o: gathering, a word for the crowd at the river
listening, a word for hearing the covenant
standing, the word that opens and names this portion

s: only the leaders stood in the covenant
the list runs from heads and elders to children, strangers and water-drawers.
Nitzavim is read on the Shabbat just before Rosh Hashanah
sometimes on its own, sometimes paired with Vayelech.

games.q: you're Moses, listing who stands in the covenant. you've named the heads, the elders and the officers. who comes next?
o: no one else: leaders speak for everyone.
children, wives, strangers, woodcutters and water-drawers.
games.why: the list runs all the way down the camp, from the heads of the tribes to the drawer of water.

practice: Think of a place you spend time, work, school, a congregation, your own home, and who makes it work without being seen: the cleaner, the night guard, the one who always notices when the dish soap runs out.
See their face if you can, and let them stand, in your mind, in the same line as the people at the front.

wordCard.voice: Nitzavim. Standing. The portion where everyone stands together, from the heads of the tribes to the drawer of water.

orig.note: Hebrew: standing, standing firm. the key word of Deuteronomy 29:9 and the name of the portion.

carryVoice: Your line: all of you. The water-drawer stands in the same sentence as the elders. Day five hundred seventeen, done.
